title: When Times Press Hard on Us
intro: The diwan introduces this as a letter to Abu Muhammad Ja'far ibn Warqa. Abu Firas wants him to arbitrate a quarrel with Ja'far’s uncle, Abu Ahmad Abd Allah ibn Warqa. The opening inventory of swords and camels gives way to a private grievance. The letter ends with the words Ja'far is to take to his uncle.

translation: When times press hard on us
and a calamity strikes and grows dark,
1.sharh: The opening “we” brings his whole household into the letter. The sentence waits for the next verse to disclose what a visitor would find there in a crisis.

translation: you find around our houses
the equipment of courage and generosity.
2.sharh: He makes two virtues visible as things stored outside the houses. The visitor can take an inventory before the poet tells him what each item is for.

translation: For meeting enemies, bright swords,
for giving freely, red camels.
3.sharh: The two colours inventory what the household owns. Camels were wealth that could actually be handed over, so their presence makes the claim about generosity concrete.

translation: Both are our custom.
One blood-debt is paid, another life is taken.
4.sharh: Blood is counted twice. A payment can settle a killing and avert retaliation, while combat spills fresh blood. The handling of a dispute already matters before the letter names one.

translation: Tell Ja'far ibn Warqa,
so he may speak from what he knows,
5.sharh: The impersonal catalogue gives way to a named witness. Ja'far is asked to speak from first-hand knowledge of the people whose conduct he must judge.

translation: that though the journey to visit is long
and my home is far from yours,
6.sharh: Distance delays the main verb as well as the visit. The English sentence, like the Arabic letter, must cross into the next verse to learn what persists.

translation: I long for those qualities
and choose those traits above others.
7.sharh: “Those” assumes that both men know the qualities in question. Longing is spontaneous, while his second verb describes a deliberate choice.

translation: I blame the assault of separation,
with pain lodged deep inside me.
8.sharh: Separation acts like an attacker. After opening with the equipment for repelling an enemy, he locates the wound inside himself.

translation: Perhaps time will turn again.
Perhaps a scattered people will come together.
9.sharh: Each “perhaps” gives reconciliation another chance. The verb for reunion can also describe a wound closing, answering the pain inside him in the previous verse.

translation: Will you one day do me justice
against your uncle’s wrong, cousin?
10.sharh: Ja'far’s uncle is the other party. Calling the judge “cousin” makes the difficulty of judging one’s own circle audible in the appeal itself.

translation: Tell him on my behalf what I say.
You are someone no one would suspect.
11.sharh: The uncle is the person who must hear this. Ja'far can carry the message as well as arbitrate because his account will be trusted.

translation: I have accepted, however much you dislike it,
Abu Muhammad as judge.
12.sharh: Abu Muhammad is Ja'far’s own kunya. His uncle learns who Abu Firas has accepted as arbitrator from the very man named to judge the dispute.

1.2.2.head: نابَ
1.2.2.meaning: Said of a calamity that befalls someone.

1.2.4.head: اِدلَهَمَّ
1.2.4.meaning: To grow dark. A crisis can “darken” until no way out is visible.

2.2.1.head: عُدَّة
2.2.1.meaning: Equipment or provisions kept ready for an occasion. The poem uses the plural.

3.1.1.head: لِقاء
3.1.1.meaning: Meeting or confronting. The final hamza of liqa' is dropped here to fit the metre.

4.2.1.head: وَدى
4.2.1.meaning: To pay compensation for a killing to the victim’s kin. The verb here is passive.

5.1.3.head: وَرقاء
5.1.3.meaning: Warqa', the name of Ja'far’s father. The recited form drops the final hamza to fit the metre.

6.1.3.head: شَطَّ
6.1.3.meaning: To lie far off, here of the place one would like to visit.

6.2.5.meaning: Near at hand, within easy reach.

7.2.4.head: شيمَة
7.2.4.meaning: A settled trait of character. The verse uses the plural.

8.1.2.head: عادِيَة
8.1.2.meaning: An assault or hostile onslaught, here attributed to separation.

9.2.2.head: شَعب
9.2.2.meaning: A body of people held together by kinship or a shared interest.

9.2.3.head: اِلتَأَمَ
9.2.3.meaning: To join back together, as the edges of a wound do.

12.2.2-3.head: أَبو مُحَمَّد
12.2.2-3.meaning: The kunya of Ja'far ibn Warqa, the arbitrator named in the letter.
